section.title: Who May Dwell on Your Holy Hill
section.sectionRationale: A short entrance liturgy, likely used as worshipers approached the tabernacle or temple, asking who may abide in God's presence and answering with a character portrait of integrity in speech, dealing with neighbors, and use of money. It functions as a searching mirror for anyone approaching worship, and pairs naturally with Psalm 24's similar entrance question.
section.thesis: Entry into God's presence is pictured through a life of integrity, truthfulness, and neighbor love, a portrait no one keeps perfectly on their own, which drives the worshiper toward the one who alone fulfills it completely.
section.frameNote: Two movements: the opening question, who may dwell with God; and the answering portrait of the one who may, described in speech, dealings, and use of money.

units.label: Who may dwell on Your holy mountain?

verses.text: O LORD, who may abide in Your tent? Who may dwell on Your holy mountain?

He who walks with {{tamim|integrity}} and practices righteousness, 
who speaks the truth from his heart,

who has no slander on his tongue, who does no harm to his neighbor, 
who casts no scorn on his friend,

who despises the vile but honors those who fear the LORD, 
who does not revise a costly oath,

who lends his money without interest and refuses a bribe against the innocent. 
He who does these things will never be {{mot|shaken}}.

tamim.gloss: Integrity, blamelessness, wholeness, completeness of character in which a person's inner life and outward conduct match. It does not mean sinless perfection but a settled, undivided honesty before God and others.

mot.gloss: To slip, totter, be shaken or overthrown. The psalm's closing promise is that the one who lives this way will never be mot, will stand firm and secure, a stability grounded in God rather than in circumstances.

basic.context: The psalm opens with a question every worshiper approaching God's presence must ask, who may actually dwell with You. The answer is not a ritual requirement but a character portrait: a person of integrity who speaks truth, does no harm with tongue or hand, keeps promises even at cost, and handles money honestly. Such a person, the psalm says, will never be shaken.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a liturgy meant to search the conscience of every worshiper before entering God's presence, not a checklist anyone fully passes on their own merit. Read alongside the rest of Scripture, it exposes the gap between the entrance requirement and our actual lives, driving us to the one person who has walked this portrait perfectly, Jesus Christ.
basic.originalLanguages: The person who may dwell with God walks in tamim, integrity or wholeness, an undivided honesty between inner life and outward conduct. The promised result is that such a person will never be mot, shaken or toppled, because their stability rests in the God they walk with, not in favorable circumstances.
basic.typology: The full and perfect portrait of tamim, integrity, is fulfilled only in Christ, the one truly blameless man, whose righteousness is now given to all who trust Him so that they too may stand unshaken on God's holy hill.
basic.christ: No one keeps this portrait perfectly on their own, which is exactly why the gospel is good news: Jesus Christ walked in complete integrity, spoke only truth, never wronged a neighbor, and kept every costly promise even to His own death, and now His righteousness, not our performance, is what grants us access to dwell with God.
basic.god: God is holy, dwelling on a mountain that requires a certain kind of life to approach, yet He is also the one who, in Christ, supplies exactly the righteousness this psalm requires so that sinners might be welcomed rather than turned away.
basic.crossReferences: Psalm 24:3-4 asks the same entrance question with a similar answer. Hebrews 10:19-22 shows believers now have confident access to God's presence through Christ's blood. Micah 6:8 summarizes similar practical righteousness expected of God's people.
basic.oneStory: This psalm's entrance liturgy shows what true fellowship with God requires and how far short every person falls, setting up the entire story's movement toward Christ, who fulfills this portrait completely and opens the way for all who trust Him to dwell with God forever.

context.literary:
The psalm has the plainest design in the Psalter: one question and one answer. Verse 1 asks in two matched lines, 'who may abide in Your tent?' and 'Who may dwell on Your holy mountain?' Verses 2 to 5 answer, and the last half of verse 5 closes with a promise. Nothing else is in it. There is no complaint, no enemy, no praise, and no prayer for help. The psalm exists to ask one question and to answer it with a portrait.

The answer is built as a list, and the list is arranged more carefully than it looks. Verse 2 gives three positive marks, a walk, a practice and a way of speaking. Verse 3 gives three negatives that widen outward from the mouth: no slander on the tongue, no harm done to a neighbour, no scorn cast on a friend. The path runs from what is said, to what is done, to what is passed on about others. Verse 4 has a pair of contrasts about loyalties, the vile despised and the God-fearing honoured, followed by a costly oath kept. Verse 5 ends with money, first lending without interest, then refusing a bribe. The list travels from the inner life, through speech and friendship, to public promises and finally to the wallet and the courtroom.

The descriptions are mostly participles, a run of present, habitual actions rather than commands. The psalm does not say 'do these things'. It says, in effect, that the person who lives like this may dwell there. That gives it the feel of a character sketch instead of a code, and it is why later Jewish tradition could count eleven marks in verses 2 to 5 and treat them as a summary of the whole Law.

Notice too what is absent. There is no mention of sacrifice, Sabbath, food laws or ritual washing. The examination concerns the tongue, the neighbour and the purse. The final promise, 'will never be shaken', returns to the image of a secure dwelling from the first line. The verb it uses for being shaken is the one Psalm 16:8 uses of David, 'I will not be shaken,' so the psalm next door describes a man who is already living what Psalm 15 promises.
context.historical:
The psalm imagines a worshiper at the gate of the sanctuary and a voice asking who is fit to go in. Israel's worship had such moments. Psalm 118:19-20 preserves one, 'Open to me the gates of righteousness ... This is the gate of the LORD; the righteous shall enter through it.' Psalm 24:3-6 is the closest parallel, and both Isaiah 33:14-16 and Ezekiel 18:5-9 give similar lists of conduct. In each case the sanctuary's threshold is a place where a person's way of life is measured.

The 'tent' of verse 1 may point to the tent David pitched in Jerusalem for the ark, 2 Samuel 6:17. Earlier, David had learned how serious it was to approach the ark carelessly, for Uzzah was struck down when he touched it, 2 Samuel 6:6-7, and David responded with fear, 'How can the ark of the LORD ever come to me?' 2 Samuel 6:9. A psalm that asks who may abide with the LORD fits that moment, although the psalm does not say so and the setting is a guess.

The specific sins of the list belong to life in a village economy. Slander could destroy a person in a community where reputation was everything, as when Mephibosheth was slandered to the king, 2 Samuel 19:27. Lending was often a matter of survival for a poor family in a bad year, and Israel's law forbade charging a fellow Israelite interest on such a loan, Exodus 22:25, Leviticus 25:36-37 and Deuteronomy 23:19-20. Nehemiah later fought the abuse of exactly this, Nehemiah 5:10-12. Bribes bought verdicts at the city gate, where cases were judged, and the Law warned that a bribe 'blinds those who see and twists the words of the righteous,' Exodus 23:8. Oaths were sworn at the altar and were serious, 1 Kings 8:31-32. The picture is of a person whose religion shows in whom he can be trusted with words, promises and money.
context.canonical:
Psalm 15 belongs to a small family of texts that ask who may stand before God. Psalm 24:3-6 asks it in almost the same words and answers with 'clean hands and a pure heart,' and Isaiah 33 places the question in the mouths of terrified sinners in Zion, 'Who of us can dwell with a consuming fire?' Isaiah 33:14, before giving its own answer in verses 15 and 16. Micah 6:6-8 asks what the LORD requires and answers, 'to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God,' in words that read like a summary of Psalm 15. Psalm 26 and Psalm 101 speak of walking 'with integrity' in the same voice.

The Psalter places Psalm 15 at the head of a run of psalms that reach a second entrance liturgy in Psalm 24, and it is followed directly by Psalm 16, in which David says he will not be shaken and expects to see the path of life.

The New Testament takes the question seriously and answers it in a way the psalm anticipates but does not state. James warns that 'whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles at just one point is guilty of breaking all of it,' James 2:10. Paul says that 'all who rely on works of the law are under a curse,' Galatians 3:10, and then that 'Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us,' Galatians 3:13. Hebrews then announces the outcome: believers 'have come to Mount Zion,' Hebrews 12:22, with 'confidence to enter the Most Holy Place by the blood of Jesus,' Hebrews 10:19. Yet the old question does not vanish. The book of Revelation says 'nothing unclean will ever enter' the new city, Revelation 21:27, and 'blessed are those who wash their robes, so that they may have the right to the tree of life and may enter the city by its gates,' Revelation 22:14. The psalm's question runs from Zion to the new Jerusalem.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The psalm was written to sharpen a worshiper's conscience at the moment of approach. David, or whoever the psalm was handed to, meant Israel to hold a conviction that sits uncomfortably beside a lot of religion: that God cares how a man speaks about his neighbour, whether he keeps a promise that costs him, and what he does with his money. A person could bring a perfect sacrifice and still be unfit if his tongue was destroying a friend.

The psalm also meant to set the pattern of a healthy community. By listing what the fit worshiper does, it describes what a covenant people would be like if they lived it out: truthful, safe to be around, loyal to those who fear the LORD, dependable in a bargain, generous to the poor and incorruptible in court. The last line was meant as an encouragement, not only a warning: those who live this way have a stability that does not depend on their circumstances. The first hearers were to go into the sanctuary humbled, aware that their entrance was a kindness, and ready to live differently when they left.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm describes a kind of person and, by implication, prescribes the kind of life God's people should seek. It is not a set of rules for gaining entry by achievement. In Israel's own understanding, the people already belonged to God by His rescue in the exodus, and the portrait describes the life of someone who lives inside that relationship. The specific examples, such as lending without interest, are given as instances of a principle, not as a full legal code. The principle is that a worshiper does not exploit those weaker than himself.

For today, the psalm calls believers to examine their speech, promises and money with the same seriousness they bring to worship, and to expect the two to be connected. It should not be read as a checklist that a person can pass to earn God's welcome, and it should not be turned into a reason to keep others out. Read with the New Testament, its portrait is a description of the life the Spirit produces in those who have been welcomed through Christ, and a standing reminder that being welcomed and being changed belong together.

debates.question: Is this psalm a condition for entering God's presence, or a description of those who already belong to Him?

views.label: It describes the fruit of covenant faithfulness, not a means of earning access
views.case: Israel's relationship with God rested on grace, on the exodus and the covenant at Sinai, before any law was given. The psalm describes what a covenant member looks like, and 'will never be shaken' reads as a promise to the faithful rather than a wage. Psalm 24:5 says such a person receives 'blessing from the LORD and vindication from the God of his salvation.'

views.label: It sets a real, searching test that worshipers were meant to take seriously
views.case: The specificity of the list, no slander, no harm, no revised oaths, no interest, no bribes, suggests that people were meant to examine themselves before entering. Isaiah 33:14 shows what an honest hearer of such a list feels: terror, 'Who of us can dwell with a consuming fire?'

debates.bearing: Both readings agree the psalm searches the conscience seriously. The Christian reading adds that no one meets the portrait unaided, and that Christ's righteousness is credited to believers, Philippians 3:9, so that they may enter.

debates.question: Does 'lends his money without interest' forbid all interest today?

views.label: It forbids exploitation of the poor, and the principle applies wherever lending is used to profit from need
views.case: The Law prohibits interest on loans to a poor fellow Israelite, Exodus 22:25 and Leviticus 25:36-37, and Nehemiah 5:10-12 shows the abuse being condemned. In a modern economy where loans fund business and not survival, the concern is to prevent oppression rather than to ban every return on capital.

views.label: It is a lasting command that should shape how believers lend among themselves
views.case: Deuteronomy 23:19-20 speaks of loans of money, food or 'any other' kind, and some Christians and Jews have read the prohibition as binding wherever a brother is lent to. On this view the psalm's ideal is generosity in lending, not the profit that interest brings, and Jesus takes the same line in Luke 6:34-35 by telling His followers to lend 'expecting nothing in return.'

debates.bearing: Both views hear the psalm's call to use money for the good of a neighbour in need. The disagreement is over how far the ancient rule is a rule for all time, and the shared point is that no one may profit from another's distress.

debates.question: Who is being asked, and what kind of text is this?

views.label: An entrance liturgy sung between worshipers and priests at the gates
views.case: The form of question and answer, and the parallel with Psalm 24, suggest a dialogue at the threshold in which a priest instructed pilgrims. Psalm 118:19-20 shows the gates were places for such exchanges.

views.label: A wisdom poem for instruction, not tied to a ritual
views.case: Nothing in the psalm mentions a gate, a priest or a procession. It could simply be a teaching psalm that uses the picture of the sanctuary to portray the righteous life, in the manner of Proverbs.

debates.bearing: The meaning is the same either way: the life that suits the presence of God is a life of truth and integrity, and the psalm teaches it to a listening congregation.

study.originalLanguages:
The first verse uses two verbs for being with God. The BSB's 'abide' is from the root gur, to live as a sojourner or resident guest, and the same verb appears in Psalm 61:4, 'Let me dwell in Your tent forever.' The worshiper is pictured as a guest under someone else's roof, welcomed and dependent. The second verb, 'dwell', comes from shakan, the root that gives the Hebrew name of the tabernacle itself, the mishkan, and it describes coming to rest in a place where God settles. The pair says that the LORD is the host, and the question is who is fit to be His guest.

Verses 2 to 5 are largely built on participles, forms that describe someone in the middle of doing something as a habit. 'He who walks with integrity' is a person who is walking, not one who has walked once. The Hebrew for 'practices righteousness' is literally 'does righteousness', an ordinary verb for making or doing, so that righteousness is treated as something a person does day after day and not only as a status. This is why the portrait reads as a character rather than a set of rules, and why the person who fails in one point falls short of the whole picture.

The verb behind 'slander' in verse 3 is built on the noun for 'foot', and describes someone who goes about with talk, carrying a report around. It appears when Ziba says that Mephibosheth has slandered him to the king, 2 Samuel 19:27. Leviticus 19:16 forbids the same activity, 'You must not go about spreading slander among your people.' The first mark of the fit worshiper is that he does not travel with other people's faults.

Verse 4 begins with a line that is literally passive: 'in whose eyes a rejected one is despised.' The word for 'vile' means one rejected or cast off, in this case by God's standards. It does not say the worshiper is contemptuous of people; it says his values are so aligned with God's that he does not honour what God rejects. The next half-line, that he 'honors those who fear the LORD', is the positive side.

The word for 'interest' in verse 5 is neshekh, which comes from a verb meaning 'to bite'. It appears in Exodus 22:25 and Leviticus 25:36-37, and the picture is of a loan that bites the borrower. The word for 'bribe' is shochad, which Exodus 23:8 says 'blinds those who see and twists the words of the righteous.' The psalm names the two ways money most easily corrupts: by biting the poor and by buying the judge. The closing promise, 'will never be shaken', uses the verb mot, which speaks of totter or slip, and the sense is of a person on a foundation that does not give way.

typology.type: The tent and the holy mountain
typology.fulfillment: The psalm asks who may abide in the LORD's tent and dwell on His mountain, and the tabernacle answered with distance: a courtyard, a veil, a priest who could enter only on one day. In Christ the dwelling comes to the people. 'The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us,' John 1:14, and those who trust Him 'have come to Mount Zion, to the city of the living God,' Hebrews 12:22. The correspondence is between God's dwelling place and the way in; the escalation is that the way in is opened by a person. The type falls short because the tent stood for a place, while Christ is the presence itself, Revelation 21:3.

typology.type: The one who walks with integrity
typology.fulfillment: The portrait of the blameless man, truthful, harmless to his neighbour and unbribable, has never been drawn from life apart from one person. Peter says of Christ, 'He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in His mouth,' 1 Peter 2:22, and Hebrews calls Him 'holy, innocent, undefiled, set apart from sinners,' Hebrews 7:26. The type is not a prediction but an unmet standard, and it finds its fulfilment where the ideal is met in a life. It falls short of the whole story because Christ does not merely display the pattern; He shares its result with the undeserving, Romans 4:5.

typology.type: The oath that costs and is not revised
typology.fulfillment: The worshiper of the psalm keeps his word even when it hurts. Christ kept His to the end. In the garden He prayed, 'not as I will, but as You will,' Matthew 26:39, and He became 'obedient to death, even death on a cross,' Philippians 2:8. The Father's own oath stands behind the same promise, for God 'swore by Himself,' Hebrews 6:13, so that His people could be sure. The correspondence is a promise held at great cost; the escalation is that the cost was His own life, and the type falls short because human oaths can only bind one person, while His binds all who trust Him.

The psalm honours the one who gives and asks no profit from the poor. Christ 'though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor, so that you through His poverty might become rich,' 2 Corinthians 8:9. He also told His followers to 'lend to them, expecting nothing in return,' Luke 6:35. The correspondence is generosity that does not bite, and the escalation is a gift of a whole inheritance to those who could never repay it. The type falls short because the psalm's lender still keeps his principal, while Christ gave Himself.

study.christ:
Psalm 15 leads to Christ by the way of a question the psalm cannot answer for itself. It asks who may dwell on God's holy mountain and gives a portrait that no one in the Old Testament fully fits, not David, whose own story includes broken promises and blood on his hands, and not any priest or king who followed. The psalm's honesty about the standard is part of its work: it leaves the reader in the position of Isaiah 33:14, asking, 'Who of us can dwell with a consuming fire?'

The New Testament answer begins with Christ Himself as the fulfilment of the portrait. He is the one who 'committed no sin, and no deceit was found in His mouth,' 1 Peter 2:22, and He could ask His accusers, 'Which of you can prove Me guilty of sin?' John 8:46. The 'truth from his heart' of verse 2 and the tongue free of slander of verse 3 are lived out in the way He 'did not retaliate' when abused, 1 Peter 2:23. The centurion at the cross said, 'Surely this was a righteous man,' Luke 23:47. Hebrews describes Him as the priest we need, 'holy, innocent, undefiled, set apart from sinners,' Hebrews 7:26.

Some of the psalm's details have a striking echo in His story. The psalm names the man who 'refuses a bribe against the innocent.' Judas took thirty pieces of silver to hand Jesus over, Matthew 26:14-16, and afterward confessed, 'I have sinned by betraying innocent blood,' Matthew 27:4. The psalm's comment on those who take money against the innocent has its most solemn illustration in the one innocent person against whom money was taken. The psalm says the fit worshiper 'does not revise a costly oath'; Jesus prayed in Gethsemane, 'not as I will, but as You will,' Matthew 26:39, and stayed on the road to the cross. And where the psalm honours the lender who does not seek profit, Paul says of Christ that 'though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor,' 2 Corinthians 8:9.

The gospel goes further than fulfilment by example. Paul says that 'all who rely on works of the law are under a curse,' Galatians 3:10, and that 'Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us,' Galatians 3:13. The entrance condition is met on our behalf: God 'made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God,' 2 Corinthians 5:21. Paul's aim is to be found in Christ, 'not having my own righteousness from the law, but that which is through faith in Christ,' Philippians 3:9, and Christ 'has become for us wisdom from God: our righteousness, holiness, and redemption,' 1 Corinthians 1:30. So the believer comes to the hill in Christ's name and is made fit for it, and then, being welcomed, begins to walk as He walked, 1 John 2:6.

A caution: Psalm 15 is not quoted in the New Testament and is not a direct prophecy. It is read this way because of what the New Testament says about the standard and about the one who met it, and it should not be treated as though each phrase speaks of Jesus in code.
study.god:
The first thing Psalm 15 shows about God is that He is the host. The tent is His, the mountain is His, and the question is put to Him, 'O LORD, who may abide in Your tent?' God is not one seeker among others, waiting to be approached by whoever likes. He sets the terms for His own house, and He does so because He is holy. 'No evil can dwell with You,' says Psalm 5:4, and that holiness is the reason a question about fitness has to be asked at all.

It also shows what God cares about, and the surprise is the ordinary shape of it. He is concerned with truth in the heart, with the tongue, with the way friends are spoken of, with promises made at a cost, with money lent and money taken. Nothing in the psalm says that these matters are more important than worship. They are the way worship is verified. A God who is holy does not confine His interest to the temple courtyard, and He takes account of what happens in the market and the courtroom. Micah puts it in his own way: 'what does the LORD require of you but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?' Micah 6:8.

God is shown as a guardian of the weak. The two economic marks, no interest on a poor man's loan and no bribe against the innocent, are about those who cannot protect themselves. The LORD who asks that these people be treated fairly is the God who stands up for them, as He does in Exodus 22:25-27 and Psalm 12:5. His holiness is not a fussiness about purity; it is a justice that reaches to the least protected.

He is faithful in a way that gives His people something to imitate. A man who does 'not revise a costly oath' is walking as God walks, since God is the one for whom 'it is impossible ... to lie' and who confirms His promises with an oath, so that 'we who have fled to take hold of the hope set before us may be strongly encouraged,' Hebrews 6:18. The keeping of one's word at cost is not merely a human ideal; it is a picture of the character of God.

He is also the source of the stability the psalm promises. 'Will never be shaken' is what David says of himself in Psalm 16:8, and in Psalm 62:2 he says of God, 'He alone is my rock and my salvation. He is my fortress; I will never be shaken.' The steadiness of the worshiper is borrowed from the One he dwells with. It is not his own.

And the psalm hints at a God who welcomes as well as examines. To ask who may dwell in His tent is to assume that some may. Psalm 24:5 says that the one who passes the test receives 'blessing from the LORD and vindication from the God of his salvation,' and Psalm 84:4 says, 'How blessed are those who dwell in Your house!' For worship, the psalm teaches reverence and honesty together: we enter God's presence knowing that He looks at our tongues, our promises and our purses, and we enter it trusting that He is the one who provides the fitness He requires.

crossReferences.note: The closest parallel: 'Who may ascend the hill of the LORD? Who may stand in His holy place?' The answer, 'clean hands and a pure heart,' is briefer than in Psalm 15 but points to the same person. Psalm 24 then says that person receives 'vindication from the God of his salvation,' which places the blessing in God's gift.

The prophet's version of the question, spoken by frightened sinners in Zion: 'Who of us can dwell with a consuming fire?' The answer, walking righteously, speaking sincerely, refusing bribes, closely parallels Psalm 15 and shows how the standard bit.

A longer list of the marks of the righteous man, including not oppressing, restoring a pledge, and not charging excess interest, which ends 'surely he will live.' It shows how the ethics of Psalm 15 were taught in the prophets.

The prophet asks what the LORD requires and answers with justice, mercy and a humble walk. It says in short what Psalm 15 says at length, that God's requirement is a way of life, not a larger offering.

The Law's rule against charging interest to a poor person among God's people. It is the root of the psalm's 'lends his money without interest,' and shows that the mark is about compassion for the needy.
'Do not accept a bribe, for a bribe blinds the eyes of the wise and twists the words of the righteous.' It gives the reason for the last mark of the psalm: a bribe corrupts justice at its source.

Uzzah's death when he touched the ark and David's fear, 'How can the ark of the LORD ever come to me?' It shows how seriously approaching God's presence was taken in David's day and supplies a possible setting for the psalm's question.

'I have set the LORD always before me. Because He is at my right hand, I will not be shaken.' The next psalm uses the same verb as the last line of Psalm 15 and shows the promise coming true in a man who trusts God.

'Since we have confidence to enter the Most Holy Place by the blood of Jesus.' It gives the New Testament answer to Psalm 15's question: believers may draw near, with a sincere heart and hearts cleansed, because of what Christ has done.
'You have come to Mount Zion, to the city of the living God.' The holy hill of Psalm 15:1 is described as a place believers have already reached, with Jesus as mediator of a new covenant.

'Nothing unclean will ever enter it ... but only those whose names are written in the Lamb's Book of Life.' The question of Psalm 15 is still answered at the end, and the answer is the Lamb's book, not the worshiper's record.

study.oneStory:
Psalm 15 asks the question that hangs over the whole Bible from Genesis 3 onward. In Eden the man and woman walked with God and were at home in His presence. When they fell, they were sent east, away from the garden, and cherubim guarded the way back, Genesis 3:24. Every page after that carries some version of the question in this psalm: who may come near?

The story then sets out the answer in stages. At Sinai God says, 'And they are to make a sanctuary for Me, so that I may dwell among them,' Exodus 25:8, and the tabernacle is built with its courtyard, its veil and its priests, so that a holy God may live beside a sinful people. But the sanctuary answers the question only in part, and the entrance liturgies of the Psalms and the prophets, Psalm 24, Isaiah 33 and Ezekiel 18, keep asking whether anyone is really fit. Psalm 15 sits in the middle of this stretch of the story and gives the honest reply: the person God receives is a truthful, harmless, faithful and generous person, and that person is rare.

Christ enters the story as the answer. He is the man who walked with integrity, without deceit, and He is also the dwelling: 'The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us,' John 1:14. He gives His people the standing the psalm demands, 'the righteousness from God on the basis of faith,' Philippians 3:9, and the veil that shut out the worshiper is opened through His body, Hebrews 10:19-20. Those who trust Him are then changed to walk as He walked, so that the psalm's portrait becomes the shape of a Spirit-formed life.

The story ends with the question answered in full. In the new creation 'the dwelling place of God is with man, and He will dwell with them,' Revelation 21:3. Nothing unclean enters, but the people who do are those who have washed their robes and have a right to the tree of life, Revelation 22:14, and they are the people of the psalm's last line, who will never be shaken, in a city whose foundations cannot move, Hebrews 12:28.

quiz.q: What question does Psalm 15 open with?

options.text: Who may abide in God's tent and dwell on His holy mountain.
options.note: This entrance question frames the entire psalm's answer.

options.text: How long will the wicked prosper.
options.note: This is a theme found elsewhere in the Psalter, such as Psalm 73, not the opening question here.

options.text: Why has God forgotten His people.
options.note: This kind of lament question appears in other psalms, but Psalm 15 opens with an entrance question, not a lament.

options.text: What sacrifice pleases God most.
options.note: The psalm's concern is ethical character rather than sacrificial ritual specifically.

quiz.q: According to verses 2-3, what marks the person fit to dwell with God?

options.text: Integrity, righteousness, truthful speech, and no slander or harm toward a neighbor.
options.note: This is the psalm's direct ethical portrait in these verses.

options.text: Wealth and social status among the people.
options.note: The psalm's criteria are ethical character, not wealth or status.

options.text: Ritual purity achieved through repeated sacrifices.
options.note: The psalm focuses on ethical conduct rather than ritual sacrifice specifically.

options.text: Physical strength and military success.
options.note: This is unrelated to the psalm's actual criteria, which concern truthful speech and harmless dealing with others.

quiz.q: What does verse 4 say about keeping oaths?

options.text: The one fit to dwell with God keeps a costly oath and does not revise it once made, even to his own hurt.
options.note: This highlights integrity that holds even when honesty costs something personally.

options.text: Oaths should always be renegotiated if circumstances change.
options.note: The psalm commends the opposite, keeping one's word even when it becomes costly.

options.text: Oaths are unnecessary for the righteous person.
options.note: The verse assumes oaths are made and specifically commends keeping them.

options.text: Only oaths made to God, not to other people, must be kept.
options.note: The psalm's broader context includes honest dealing with neighbors and friends generally, not oaths to God alone.

quiz.q: What does the psalm say about money in verse 5?

options.text: The righteous person lends without interest and refuses a bribe against the innocent.
options.note: This describes honest, non-exploitative use of money toward the vulnerable and innocent.

options.text: Money should never be lent under any circumstances.
options.note: The psalm does not forbid lending; it forbids charging interest that exploits a neighbor in need and forbids bribery.

options.text: Wealth automatically disqualifies a person from God's presence.
options.note: The psalm concerns how money is used ethically, not wealth itself as disqualifying.

options.text: Bribes are acceptable if used to help the innocent.
options.note: This misreads the verse, which explicitly refuses bribery against the innocent under any pretext.

quiz.q: How does this psalm point toward Christ?

options.text: It describes a portrait of integrity no sinner keeps perfectly, fulfilled completely only in Jesus, whose righteousness now grants believers access to dwell with God.
options.note: The psalm's high ethical bar drives the reader to the only one who meets it fully, Christ, and to grace received through Him.

options.text: It teaches that anyone can earn entrance to heaven through good works alone.
options.note: This contradicts the gospel and the broader biblical teaching that righteousness before God comes through faith in Christ.

options.text: It has no connection to the New Testament's teaching on righteousness.
options.note: The psalm's entrance theme connects clearly to New Testament teaching about access to God through Christ, as in Hebrews 10.

options.text: It predicts a specific future event unrelated to personal righteousness.
options.note: This misses the psalm's clear ethical focus, which points toward the righteousness fulfilled in Christ rather than an unrelated prediction.

questions: This psalm asks who may dwell with God and answers with a life of integrity, honest speech, and harmless dealing with others. Where does your own life fall short of this portrait, and how does that shortfall point you toward needing Christ's righteousness rather than your own?
The psalm commends someone who keeps a costly oath even to their own hurt. Where might you be tempted to break a promise or commitment because keeping it has become inconvenient or costly?
Verse 3 warns against slander and casting scorn on a friend. How do your words about others, whether in conversation or online, measure up against this standard?

The psalm commends refusing a bribe against the innocent and lending without exploiting a neighbor's need. Where in your own use of money or influence might you need to choose integrity over self-interest?

The psalm promises that the one who lives this way will never be shaken. Where do you need that kind of unshakeable security right now, and how does resting in Christ's righteousness, rather than your own performance, provide it?

translationNotes.note: Integrity renders tamim, meaning wholeness or blamelessness, an undivided honesty between inner life and outward conduct rather than sinless perfection.
Does not revise a costly oath reflects the sense of keeping one's word even when honoring it brings personal loss or hardship.
Shaken renders mot, meaning to slip, totter, or be overthrown; the promise is of settled stability grounded in relationship with God.
